explain.say: Take a round roti and a piece of string as long as its radius. Lay the string along the edge. The angle it makes at the centre is called one radian. Look at the first bar: one radian is about 57.3 degrees.

explain.say: How many strings fit round a quarter of the edge? About 1.571. See the second bar? That is pi over 2. Pi turns up because the edge of a circle is pi times its width.

explain.say: Half the edge takes 3.142 strings: exactly pi. Look at the third bar. So a half turn, 180 degrees, is pi radians. How many do you think fit all the way round?

explain.say: Two pi, about 6.283 strings, the last bar. The full edge is 2 pi r, and each string is r long, so 2 pi of them fit. That is why 360 degrees equals 2 pi radians.

explain.say: Well done! Radians measure angle with the circle's own ruler, so formulas become simple: arc length is just radius times angle. Calculus loves radians: the slope of sine is cosine only when you use them.

faq.a: A radian is the angle you get when the arc along the edge of a circle is as long as the radius. One radian is about 57.3 degrees.

faq.q: Why is a half turn pi radians?
faq.a: Half the edge of a circle is pi times the radius long. Each radian uses one radius of edge, so a half turn is pi radians.

faq.q: Why is a full turn 2 pi radians?
faq.a: The whole edge of a circle is 2 pi r long. Dividing by r, the length of one radian of arc, gives 2 pi radians.

faq.q: How do you change degrees to radians?
faq.a: Multiply by pi over 180. For example, 90 degrees times pi over 180 gives pi over 2.
asks: How do I convert degrees to radians?

faq.q: Why do we use radians in calculus?
faq.a: In radians, the derivative of sine x is exactly cosine x. In degrees an awkward factor of pi over 180 appears in every formula.
